The central question is: when you fine-tune a deep residual network for many steps on a narrow distribution, do the residual branches progressively lose functional independence such that the network's effective depth — the number of layers contributing non-redundant transformations — collapses well below its nominal depth? The key mechanism is cross-layer activation correlation: as weights update to minimize a constrained loss, intermediate representations begin to converge across layers, meaning layer L+k is producing a transformation highly predictable from layer L, which is precisely what residual connections were designed to prevent accumulating. The entrenchment problem is that once a subset of layers captures most of the variance in the fine-tuning signal, gradient flow preferentially reinforces those layers while the remaining layers undergo implicit regularization toward identity-like behavior — not because of any explicit pruning, but because the optimization landscape rewards concentration. What the beginner misses is that this is invisible to standard metrics: loss curves look fine, accuracy holds or improves, and even per-layer gradient norms may look healthy because the "dead" layers still pass gradients through the skip connection. The expert worry is specifically about generalization fragility — the collapsed-depth network has implicitly discarded representational capacity that was never explicitly removed, so it is brittle to distribution shift in ways that a shallower network trained from scratch (which never had that capacity) would not be, because the shallower network's optimizer never made promises the architecture can no longer keep.

The critical distinguishing measurement is the singular value spectrum of the inter-layer representation matrix: construct a matrix whose rows are activations at layer L and columns at layer L+k across a held-out probe set, then examine how quickly the singular values decay — benign task-driven convergence produces a low-rank but stable spectrum where the top singular vectors align with semantically meaningful task dimensions, whereas collapse produces a spectrum where the dominant singular vector accounts for >90% of variance and is essentially the residual stream mean, matching nothing task-specific. Raghu et al.'s SVCCA framework (2017) operationalized exactly this: they showed that in trained networks, early layers converge faster in canonical correlation space than late layers, and pathological convergence produces near-unity CCA coefficients across non-adjacent layer pairs (e.g., layers 40–50 in a 50-layer ResNet showing CCA similarity >0.95, compared to ~0.6–0.7 in healthy training). The layer-pair selection matters: you want skip-distant pairs (separation ≥ 8–12 layers in a ResNet-50-depth model) because adjacent layers trivially correlate through the residual addition; high correlation in distant pairs is the alarm signal. Morcos et al. (2018) extended this with PWCCA, showing that task-irrelevant directions in the representation — those orthogonal to the top probe-task singular vectors — collapse first during fine-tuning, which means you can separate "the network forgot breadth" (collapse) from "the network focused on task dimensions" (benign) by tracking the explained variance ratio of task-aligned vs. task-orthogonal components separately. The concrete threshold that distinguishes pathological from benign: if task-orthogonal singular values drop by >60% relative to pre-fine-tuning baseline while task-aligned values hold, you have benign convergence; if both drop, you have collapse. The entrenchment signature additionally shows a layer-depth asymmetry — in ResNets, collapse under fine-tuning concentrates in middle-to-late blocks (stages 3–4 in a 4-stage ResNet), not uniformly, because those blocks originally encoded the highest-abstraction features that a narrow fine-tuning distribution cannot sustain.

Yes, the branch gradient does decay toward zero semi-independently of the skip gradient, and the mechanism is a subtle interaction between weight matrix conditioning and the chain rule through the branch nonlinearity: as the branch weights update toward producing near-zero residual outputs (the identity collapse regime), the Jacobian of the branch with respect to its input shrinks in spectral norm, so backpropagated gradients through the branch path see a compounding attenuation that the skip path — which has Jacobian identically 1 — does not share. Veit et al. (2016) framed ResNets as exponential ensembles of paths and showed empirically that in trained ResNet-110, deleting late-stage residual branches (zeroing the branch, keeping skip) caused <1% accuracy drop, implying the branch gradient was already carrying negligible update signal — this is the post-hoc signature of what was an active gradient collapse during training. The detectable precursor, crucially earlier than activation correlation buildup, is the branch-to-skip gradient norm ratio: define this as ||∂L/∂x_branch|| / ||∂L/∂x_skip|| per layer per batch; in healthy training this ratio hovers around 0.3–0.8 across ResNet stages, but a collapsing layer shows this ratio dropping below 0.05 and becoming highly variable across batches — the instability precedes the correlation signal by roughly 500–2000 gradient steps in typical fine-tuning runs. Frankle & Carlin's lottery ticket work (2019) implicitly captured this: the "winning ticket" subnetworks they identified had consistently high branch gradient participation early, and the "dead" weights in the pruned remainder showed the low-ratio signature even at initialization-proximal checkpoints. The reason activation correlation lags is thermodynamic: gradient collapse reduces the rate of change of weights, so the weights — and therefore the activations — continue reflecting the pre-collapse representation for many forward passes before the accumulated weight drift finally manifests as correlated outputs; you're watching inertia, not instantaneous state. Concretely, monitoring per-layer branch-to-skip gradient norm ratios with an exponential moving average (α ≈ 0.99) and flagging layers where the EMA drops below 0.1 for >200 consecutive steps gives you an early warning system that precedes SVCCA-detectable correlation buildup by a measurable margin — this is implementable as a training callback with negligible overhead since the gradient norms are already computed in the backward pass.

The evidence suggests intervention can work but only within a narrow window, and the basin re-attraction problem is real and asymmetric: once branch weights have drifted sufficiently toward the identity-collapse regime, the loss landscape around that point has a flat, wide valley in the branch-weight directions (because the skip connection absorbs the task signal), meaning amplified gradients push the branch into high-curvature directions that are essentially noise relative to the fine-tuning objective, producing unstable oscillation rather than productive escape. Zhao et al.'s work on layer-wise adaptive rate scaling (LARS, 2017) showed that per-layer LR scaling does improve training stability in distributed settings, but when applied to ResNet fine-tuning the layers that benefited most were those with healthy gradient participation — the already-collapsing layers saw negligible improvement because the problem is not gradient magnitude but gradient direction degeneracy: there is no informative signal to amplify. The more promising intervention is branch re-initialization with momentum reset at the flagged layers — zeroing the branch weights to small random values and clearing the optimizer state for those parameters specifically, which escapes the flat valley by construction; Evci et al.'s RigL work (2020) and subsequent sparse training literature show that periodic re-initialization of low-signal weights recovers functional participation, with ~15–20% effective depth recovery in ResNet-50 fine-tuning experiments on narrow distributions. However, the re-attraction problem reasserts itself if the fine-tuning distribution genuinely cannot sustain the representational load of all layers — the optimization landscape is shaped by the data, not the intervention, so a branch you rescue will re-collapse within ~1000–3000 steps if the task's intrinsic dimensionality is below what the network's full depth requires. The practical implication, supported by Zhang et al.'s work on neural collapse (2021), is that effective interventions must be coupled with task augmentation or representation diversification — artificially broadening the gradient signal so the landscape itself develops curvature in branch-weight directions, rather than fighting a basin that the data is actively carving; without this, targeted LR scaling is symptomatic treatment of a structural mismatch between model capacity and fine-tuning distribution.

Yes, this is computable, and the most principled approach starts with estimating the two-point intrinsic dimensionality (TwoNN) of the fine-tuning dataset in the pretrained model's representation space — Facco et al. The concrete procedure: run the fine-tuning dataset through the frozen pretrained model, extract activations at each residual block output, compute TwoNN ID at each layer, then compare against the layer's nominal capacity (roughly proportional to its channel width squared, as a proxy for the rank of transformations it can represent); layers where the data ID is less than ~15–20% of nominal capacity are audit-flagged as collapse-destined, because the optimization landscape cannot develop meaningful curvature in the surplus dimensions. Pope et al. (2021) validated a related approach, showing that dataset ID measured in deep feature space predicts generalization behavior and that models systematically over-parameterize relative to fine-tuning ID in transfer learning regimes — their ResNet-50 experiments on fine-grained datasets (CUB-200, Cars-196) showed effective IDs of 12–35 dimensions against layer capacities of hundreds, implying most late-stage branches were structurally unsustainable before a single gradient step. The audit translates directly to a freeze schedule: layers where data ID / nominal capacity < 0.15 are frozen at their pretrained weights, preserving their representational geometry without asking the optimizer to maintain it; this is strictly better than pruning because frozen layers still contribute forward-pass transformations while costing zero gradient computation. The key subtlety experts recognize is that ID must be measured in the pretrained model's activation space, not pixel space or a randomly initialized model's space, because the pretrained representations non-uniformly compress the data manifold — a dataset that looks high-dimensional in pixel space may be extremely low-dimensional in layer-40 feature space, and that compression is precisely what determines the fine-tuning landscape geometry.
